Best: After the crash by Michel Bussi, translated from French into English. I picked it up on a whim in the library and it was brilliant. A plane crashes in the Alps and the only survivor is a 3-month-old girl. Two families claim her as their grand-daughter. This was before DNA testing of course. We examine the investigation nearly 20 years later. Would recommend.

Runner up: The Martian by Andy Weir. It was refreshing to see a hero dealing with the logistics of living, instead of all that stuff being assumed in the background.

Best: Confederacy of Dunces. It's hilarious, go read it. The original neckbeard.

Worst: Tried picking up literary darlings Infinite Jest, Gravity's Rainbow and White Noise. Had to drop them all before 100 pages. It's amazing how far big words and entry-level STEM will get you in the literary world. If I have to name a book I read all the way through, I'd say Americanah by Chimamanda Adichie. I read it to open my mind to this popular idea that black people are treated unfairly in the Western World. All the points she made were poorly reasoned. Yeah, Red Lining sucks for the responsible blacks- but what, should we force banks to lend at a loss? Yeah, Blacks get it rough from the justice system- but good lord, let's not burn the capitol just because you get pulled over more frequently than a white person. She forgot to include an antithesis to what she was saying, so it failed to convince me. It was, however, the first book I was satisfied approaching as a disguised essay.

It was at Histiaea that a royal messenger from Xerxes' headquarters presently reached them. On his arrival the entire expeditionary force was paraded to hear the Great King's word. This turned out to be a general invitation to come over and inspect the Thermopylae battlefield.

'Friends and fellow-soldiers,' the messenger announced, 'the king grants leave for anyone who wants to go and see with his own eyes how he fights against the madmen who thought they could beat him'. There was an immediate rush to take advantage of this offer -- so much so that the supply of boats ran out, which suggests that only small craft and transports were being used.

All next day [22 August] parties of sailors and marines, from every quarter of the Eastern Mediterranean pottered about the Hot Gates, prodding corpses and being lectured by Xerxes' officers. They were not overimpressed. To mistake dead Helots for Spartiates was the kind of error any tourist might make; but, says Herodotus, with visible relish, 'Xerxes' ludicrous attempt to conceal the number of his own dead [see here] deceived nobody.'
